title: Short Stuff: Traffic Signals
summary: Short Stuff episode on the invention of the traffic light. The hosts walk through competing claims for the first traffic signal: London's 1868 gas-lamp semaphore designed by railway engineer John Peake Knight, which exploded weeks after installation; Lester Wire's 1912 Salt Lake City birdhouse-like light; Earnest Serene's 1910 Chicago automatic arm signal (no lights); James Hoge's 1914 Cleveland four-way signal, usually credited as the first; William Gilleran's automatic light in San Francisco; William Potts of Detroit's 1920 three-color caution light; Garrett Morgan's T-shaped signal with an all-stop phase, whose patent was sold to GE; and John Allen's pedestrian walk/don't walk signal and his idea of sponsored signals. The episode also briefly mentions other early traffic firsts such as left-hand driving standardization, center lines, and the no-left-turn sign.

segments.title: Opening and framing the traffic light debate
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic of the traffic light's invention and note that the commonly cited first signal in Cleveland in 1914 is disputed. They mention shout-outs to sources and briefly cite other automotive firsts such as left-hand driving standardization, center dividing lines, and the first no-left-turn sign.

segments.title: London's 1868 gas-lamp traffic signal
segments.summary: The hosts describe London's 1868 traffic signal in Westminster, designed by railway engineer John Peake Knight using a railway semaphore design with gas lamps for night use. Operated by a police officer, it worked well until a gas lamp exploded in an officer's face about a month later, and the British abandoned it for about forty years.

segments.title: Early American patents and Chicago's 1910 automatic signal
segments.summary: Americans took up the idea in the early 1900s with many patents. Earnest Serene's 1910 automatic signal in Chicago had rotating arms like a weather vane but no lights, so the hosts do not count it as a true traffic light, though it was a groundwork for the concept.

segments.title: Lester Wire, Cleveland 1914 and James Hoge
segments.summary: Lester Wire's 1912 signal in Salt Lake City had red and green lights on a birdhouse-like wooden box attached to trolley wires. The hosts question why Cleveland's 1914 signal is still considered first, crediting James Hoge's four-way signals at Euclid and East 105th, which were coordinated so conflicting signals could not be displayed.

segments.title: Automatic lights, the caution light, Garrett Morgan and the all-stop phase
segments.summary: William Gilleran's San Francisco automatic light, which used red and green, is noted. William Potts of Detroit introduced the amber caution light around 1920. Garrett Morgan's T-shaped signal had a stop phase on all sides between changes, which he sold to GE for about forty thousand dollars, and GE mass-produced the signals, which is why Morgan is often credited as the father of the traffic signal. The all-stop overlap has since largely disappeared.

segments.title: John Allen's pedestrian signal and sponsored signals
segments.summary: John Allen created the first street-level pedestrian signal, with a walk/don't-walk design (upright palm for stop) still in use. He also proposed sponsored signals with advertising, which the hosts agree would have been unappealing.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts joke about gas pump advertisements and close the Short Stuff episode, noting it is a production of iHeart Radio.
